headline: How Kohl's lost its way — and is trying to become relevant again
blog_article:
## Signal

Kohl’s, once a staple of American retail, has seen its relevance and stock value plummet after losing touch with its core customer base. Now, the company is launching a series of repositioning efforts to regain market relevance. [(CNBC Business)](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/06/27/how-kohls-lost-its-way-and-is-trying-to-become-relevant-again.html)

## Tension

The hidden tension: Can a legacy brand attract new demographics without alienating the loyal customers who built its foundation? For Kohl’s, the risk is clear—chasing new markets may fracture the very base that sustained its growth, but standing still means irrelevance.

## Real Business Response

Retailers facing this tension have responded with a familiar toolkit: rebranding initiatives, updated product assortments, partnerships with popular brands, and investments in digital and omnichannel experiences. The goal is to broaden appeal and modernize the brand, but each move risks further disconnecting from the original customer.

## Company Example: Kohl’s

Kohl’s faced a sharp decline in sales and stock value as its traditional middle-market shoppers drifted away, squeezed by both discount retailers and trendier competitors. The company’s response: a multi-pronged repositioning. Kohl’s updated its product mix, introducing more athleisure and home goods. It partnered with brands like Sephora to draw younger shoppers. Digital transformation became a priority, with investments in omnichannel shopping and a refreshed online experience.

But the outcome remains uncertain. While these moves generated headlines and some initial foot traffic, the core question lingers: has Kohl’s truly reconnected with its original customers, or simply traded one audience for another? The risk is that in the pursuit of new relevance, the brand’s identity becomes diluted—neither resonating with legacy shoppers nor fully capturing the loyalty of new ones.

## Business Lesson

Staying attuned to the evolving preferences of your core customers is non-negotiable. Relevance in retail is fragile—once lost, it’s rarely recovered by surface-level pivots alone. Recovery demands bold, multi-faceted strategies, but the real work is internal: clarifying who you serve and why, before chasing the next market trend.

linkedin_post:
Kohl’s spent years chasing new shoppers—and woke up to find its old ones gone.

The company’s stock and sales didn’t just dip; they collapsed as the core customers who built Kohl’s loyalty drifted away.

The response? A scramble of rebrands, new product lines, trendy partnerships, and digital upgrades. All aimed at attracting younger, broader audiences.

But here’s the catch: none of those moves guarantee the old customers will come back. In fact, the risk is that Kohl’s ends up pleasing no one—neither the legacy shoppers nor the new crowd.

This isn’t just a retail problem. It’s a lesson in relevance. When you lose sight of who made you matter, chasing the next trend won’t fix the hole.

Relevance isn’t about surface-level pivots. It’s about hard choices on who you serve and why. Without that clarity, repositioning is just noise.

threads_sequence: Kohl’s didn’t lose customers. It lost its sense of who its customers were.

That confusion cost Kohl’s sales and stock value faster than any rebranding campaign could recover.
The real gap isn’t in the market. It’s in the brand’s clarity about who still matters.
